clue.text: Maybe tie pet next to English river

parts.note: to pet and to neck both mean to kiss and cuddle
the Wear is a river in north-east England, flowing through Durham

explanation.surface: Someone ties up a pet beside a river in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pet' reads as a noun being tied up, but it is the verb meaning to kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is one example of clothing worn round the neck, hence 'Maybe'.

clue.text: Emperor inert now exposed

indicators.note: something exposed has had its covering stripped away, so each word loses its outside letters

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters removed
the word with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: A once-active emperor is now shown up as idle.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was a Roman emperor of the first century AD, famed for fiddling while Rome burned.

clue.text: Animal shelter: place to sleep and recuperate ultimately

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: An animal shelter offers a bed where a creature can rest and recover.
explanation.definitionFit: A cote is a small shed or pen for birds or animals, as in dovecote.

clue.text: Having a job lot somewhere in Cumbria

parts.note: someone with a job is working
a ton, informally, is a lot, as in 'tons of time'

explanation.surface: Plenty of people have jobs somewhere in north-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: Cumbria is a county in north-west England; Workington is a town on its coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Workington is a coastal town in that English county, so it is a place located there.

clue.text: Medicinal plant Isaac, in rain, partly lifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters means reading them from bottom to top
partly means only a portion of the words is used, a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the end of Isaac, all of in, and the start of rain

explanation.surface: Isaac's medicinal plant gets raised up out of the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnica is a mountain flower in the daisy family whose extract is used to treat bruises.

clue.text: Incentive increases revolutionary resistance

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns round, so the word before it is read backwards

parts.note: ups, as a verb, means increases
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A motive grows stronger as rebels resist.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur is something that urges on, like the spike a rider uses on a horse.

clue.text: Time off grid in hole

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters of the next word are rearranged
in places the jumbled letters inside the word that follows

parts.note: a pore is a tiny hole in the skin
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone takes time off the electricity grid, living in a hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' here is British slang for a prison sentence, and so is porridge, as in the sitcom of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing porridge is British slang for serving a jail sentence, i.e. doing time.

clue.text: Mull and another Hebridean island popular at start of Easter

parts.note: Rum is one of the Small Isles of the Inner Hebrides
in means fashionable or popular
taken as written

indicators.note: start of tells us to keep just the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A traveller lists Hebridean islands that are popular to visit around Easter.
explanation.walkthrough: Mull looks like the first of a pair of islands, but it is the verb meaning to think over; Rum is the other island.
explanation.definitionFit: To mull something over and to ruminate both mean to ponder it at length.

clue.text: Modest group of soldiers becoming weary

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
growing tired

explanation.surface: A humble group of soldiers grows tired.
explanation.definitionFit: A retiring person is shy and self-effacing, avoiding attention.

clue.text: Penny to drive vehicle containing baby?

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for a penny
to ram is to drive or force in

explanation.surface: Penny is going to drive a car with a baby on board.
explanation.walkthrough: A pram is the British word for a baby carriage pushed by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A pram is a wheeled carriage for an infant, a vehicle with a baby inside.

clue.text: Oil company missing leader, old German stargazer

indicators.note: missing leader says the word loses its first letter

parts.note: Castrol is a well-known British brand of motor oil
O is the standard abbreviation for old
GER is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: An oil firm without its boss turns to an elderly German star-reader.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrologer studies the stars to predict events, so is a gazer at them.

clue.text: Field event is turning on debate

parts.note: the discus throw is an athletics field event

indicators.note: turning round sends the word just before it in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written, then read backwards
taken as written

explanation.surface: An athletics event is now the subject of debate.
explanation.definitionFit: A discussion is a conversation in which views are argued, a synonym for debate.

clue.text: Troops do supply means of controlling entrance

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, supply means flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order

parts.note: the letters of both words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Soldiers provide a way of controlling who comes in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like the verb to provide, but it is read as 'in a supple way'.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorstop holds a door in place, so it governs whether an opening stays open or shut.

clue.text: Arsenal match programme for example

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a store of weapons and ammunition
second meaning: a periodical publication, of which a match programme is one kind

explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal and 'match programme' suggest the London football club, but the first word is just a weapons store.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a military storehouse for munitions and a printed periodical with articles.

clue.text: Shade over cooking apparatus

parts.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
a range is a large kitchen stove

explanation.surface: A dark shade has been spread across the stove.
explanation.definitionFit: Orange is a colour, and a shade is a particular colour or hue.

clue.text: Bachelor suitably optimistic

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA
right, as an adverb, means properly or suitably

explanation.surface: A single man is fittingly hopeful about the future.
explanation.definitionFit: A bright outlook is a hopeful one, so the adjective is a synonym of optimistic.

clue.text: Fully developed horse crossing turf half-cropped

indicators.note: crossing means going across, so one piece straddles and encloses the other

parts.note: a mare is a female horse

indicators.note: cropped by half means the word loses half its letters, the back two

parts.note: taken as written, then cut back

explanation.surface: A grown horse crosses a lawn whose grass has been half trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Mature means grown to full size or ripeness, having reached complete development.

clue.text: Fair senora at sea recalled Mediterranean island

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the Spanish word for a married woman, rearranged

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the island's name is read in the backwards direction

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island where Napoleon was exiled

explanation.surface: A fair Spanish lady on a cruise remembers a Mediterranean island.
explanation.definitionFit: Reasonable means fair and sensible, as in a fair or reasonable price.

clue.text: Stick with good blouse that's used regularly

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good

indicators.note: used regularly means only every other letter of the word is taken

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone keeps wearing the same good blouse every day.
explanation.definitionFit: To glue something is to fix it in place with adhesive, so it is a verb synonym of stick.

clue.text: Charlie, tense comic

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
a wit is a witty person, a joker or comic

explanation.surface: Charlie is a nervous comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'right charlie' is a fool, so the name here is an ordinary noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie is informal British slang for a silly person, as is twit.

clue.text: Gaunt husband imprisoned in can

indicators.note: something imprisoned is shut inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a tin is a can
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A skinny husband is locked up in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' is also slang for prison, which suits the surface but here it means a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaunt means haggard and lean, which is a sense of thin.

clue.text: Cork area with ground-level residence

parts.note: a bung is a stopper, like a cork
A is the abbreviation for area
at ground level is low down

explanation.surface: A home in County Cork with everything on the ground floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Cork suggests the Irish city or county, but it is a stopper; 'ground-level' does double duty in the surface, describing the single-storey house.
explanation.definitionFit: A bungalow is a single-storey house, so it is a kind of residence.

clue.text: Quick look back in swamp — I'm scared

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word
eek is a cry of fright

explanation.surface: Someone glances back in a marsh and squeals with fear.
explanation.definitionFit: A peek is a brief, furtive glance, a quick look.

clue.text: Mike retires unexpectedly, in the best of spirits

indicators.note: unexpectedly suggests things not happening in the planned order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the word, rearranged

explanation.surface: Mike stops work early and could not be happier about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Merriest is the superlative of merry, meaning most cheerful, matching the superlative definition.
